summary: The xDrive25e is the first plug-in hybrid X1 BMW Australia has sold locally, added mid-2026 as the only PHEV in a range that otherwise runs mild-hybrid petrol or the battery-electric iX1. It pairs the base car's 1.5-litre three-cylinder with an 80kW motor and a 14.2kWh usable battery for 180kW, 6.8sec to 100km/h and a WLTP electric range BMW Australia quotes at 78-86km depending on specification, enough to cover most Melbourne commutes on grid power. Reviewers rate the underlying X1 highly (CarExpert's Best Luxury Small SUV two years running, and CarsGuide scored the xDrive25e 8.0 as the premium small SUV benchmark), but CarsGuide saw only about 55km of real-world electric range and 9.5-10L/100km once flat, so the case over the cheaper petrol or the FBT-exempt iX1 rests on tax and home charging rather than driving.
pros: 78-86km of WLTP electric range from a 14.2kWh usable battery clears the daily commute for most buyers in a genuinely premium small SUV, against 76km for the Mazda CX-60 PHEV

At $79,900 before on-roads it sits $909 under the ordinary $80,809 LCT threshold, so no luxury car tax applies at all, and at 56g/km WLTP CO2 it is comfortably inside Victoria's 120g/km green passenger car limit, so stamp duty is charged at the green rate
180kW and 477Nm for 6.8sec to 100km/h makes it the second-quickest X1 behind the $94,700 M35i, and well ahead of the $67,500 sDrive20i Xline
1,700kg braked towing is unusually strong for a compact PHEV and matches the Cupra Formentor VZe; many small plug-ins are rated at 750kg or not at all
Five-year unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional and not tied to servicing inside the BMW network, with the high-voltage battery separately covered for eight years or 160,000km
cons: The battery costs the X1 50 litres of boot, dropping it from 540 litres in the petrol car to 490, and Carwow notes the plug-in is the smallest boot in the whole X1 line-up, below even the mild-hybrid grades

Once the battery is flat it is a 1.5-litre three-cylinder hauling roughly 1,855kg: ADAC's WLTP battery-empty figure is 6.1L/100km and CarsGuide measured 9.5-10L/100km in real driving, so the running-cost case collapses for anyone who cannot charge at home

It lost the FBT exemption that PHEVs held until 1 April 2025, while the battery-electric iX1 xDrive30 M Sport at around $86,800 keeps it; on a novated lease that roughly $6,900 gap can be outweighed entirely

Charging is AC-only at 11kW with no DC capability, so a flat battery is a one-hour-45-minute stop on a wallbox and cannot be topped up usefully on the road; the Cupra Formentor VZe offers 50kW DC for $10,910 less
Only one grade is offered and the M Sport package with 19-inch wheels is mandatory, which pushes the car to the low end of BMW's 78-86km range band and leaves no cheaper entry point into the X1 PHEV
